evidence.quote: the highway curves northeastward around Red Rock Canyon to the Las Vegas city limits

evidence.claim: Charleston Boulevard

evidence.claim: sandstone cliffs
evidence.quote: red- and cream-colored sandstone cliffs

evidence.claim: a ranch
evidence.quote: The state park preserves the historic Sandstone Ranch

evidence.claim: a gypsum town
evidence.quote: The nearby gypsum mine was purchased in 1923 by the Blue Diamond Corporation of California. The company opened a wallboard manufacturing plant at the site in 1941, and then began building a company town in 1942.

evidence.claim: West of Las Vegas, SR 159 changes from the urban Charleston Boulevard corridor to a rural two-lane road curving beneath Red Rock Canyon.
evidence.quote: The first segment is a rural two-lane highway

evidence.claim: urban Charleston Boulevard corridor
evidence.quote: An at-grade intersection with Sky Vista Drive reveals the first signblades for Charleston Boulevard.

evidence.claim: The Wilson Cliffs stand to the west, and the road crosses Cottonwood Valley.
evidence.quote: State Route 159 cuts through the Cottonwood Valley, also a side trail of the Old Spanish Trail. The Wilson Cliffs, a massive escarpment, can be seen to the west from SR 159.

evidence.claim: Approximately 8.8 miles of SR 159 in Red Rock Canyon became a Nevada Scenic Byway on June 30, 1995.
evidence.quote: Approximately 8.8 miles (14.2 km) of SR 159 in Red Rock Canyon was designated a Nevada Scenic Byway on June 30, 1995.

evidence.claim: BLM highlights the conservation area's red- and cream-colored sandstone cliffs and its hiking and climbing terrain.
evidence.quote: Visit the red- and cream-colored sandstone cliffs and experience the natural wonders of the Mohave Desert just 17 miles west of the Las Vegas Strip.

evidence.claim: hiking and climbing terrain.
evidence.quote: Red Rock National Conservation Area features world-class climbing, miles of hiking trails

evidence.claim: Travel through Cottonwood Valley long predates the highway designation.
evidence.quote: The spring-fed creek and grassy meadows formed an oasis for travelers using the alternate route of the Spanish Trail through Cottonwood Valley.

evidence.claim: In the mid-1830s, a campsite developed beside the spring-fed creek at what is now Spring Mountain Ranch.
evidence.quote: In the mid-1830s, a campsite was established along the wash that runs through the ranch.

evidence.claim: Pack and wagon trains used the site until rail travel replaced them in 1905.
evidence.quote: The use of the site by pack and wagon trains continued until their replacement by the railroad in 1905.

evidence.claim: Farther along the valley, gypsum production brought another change: a wallboard plant opened in 1941, followed by construction of the Blue Diamond company town in 1942.
evidence.quote: The company opened a wallboard manufacturing plant at the site in 1941, and then began building a company town in 1942.

evidence.claim: Blue Diamond occupies the site of Cottonwood Spring, a watering place on the Old Spanish Trail and the later Mormon Road.
evidence.quote: Blue Diamond is the site of Cottonwood Spring (formerly known as Ojo de Cayetana, or Pearl Spring), a watering place and campsite on the Old Spanish Trail and the later Mormon Road

evidence.claim: Driving from the Summerlin South side toward Blue Diamond, the road curves around Red Rock Canyon.
evidence.quote: From there, the highway curves northeastward around Red Rock Canyon to the Las Vegas city limits west of the Las Vegas Beltway. As it enters the census-designated place of Summerlin South

evidence.claim: The 13-mile Scenic Loop is a separate one-way excursion from SR 159.
evidence.quote: A one-way, loop road, 13 miles (21 km) long, provides vehicle access to many of the features in the area.

evidence.claim: a separate one-way excursion from SR 159.
evidence.quote: Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area is located 17 miles west of the Las Vegas Strip on Charleston Boulevard/State Route 159.

evidence.claim: The ranch lies five miles northwest of the town.
evidence.quote: Spring Mountain Ranch State Park is a public recreation area located within the Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area in Nevada's Cottonwood Valley, five miles (8.0 km) northwest of Blue Diamond, Nevada.

evidence.claim: Continue toward Spring Mountain Ranch State Park, then Blue Diamond and the junction with SR 160.
evidence.quote: The first segment is a rural two-lane highway that begins at its junction with SR 160 (Pahrump Valley Highway, Blue Diamond Road) and Erskine Junction Way.

evidence.claim: Continue toward Spring Mountain Ranch State Park, then Blue Diamond
evidence.quote: the highway proceeds northwesterly through the town of Blue Diamond toward Spring Mountain Ranch State Park.

evidence.claim: The Scenic Loop begins at the visitor center and travels one way for 13 miles.
evidence.quote: A one-way, loop road, 13 miles (21 km) long, provides vehicle access to many of the features in the area.

evidence.claim: begins at the visitor center
evidence.quote: A visitor center is at the start of the loop road.

evidence.claim: A moderate opening climb gives way to mostly downhill or level driving.
evidence.quote: it begins with a moderate climb, then is mostly downhill or flat.

evidence.claim: Near the northern section, huge sandstone blocks remain from the Excelsior Company's early-20th-century quarry.
evidence.quote: In the early 20th century, around the time the first European Americans settled in nearby Las Vegas, the Excelsior Company operated a small sandstone quarry near the northern area of the scenic loop.

evidence.claim: huge sandstone blocks remain
evidence.quote: Evidence of the quarry's existence includes some of the huge sandstone blocks that have been left behind.

evidence.claim: The operation closed because it was uneconomical.
evidence.quote: It proved to be uneconomical and was shut down.

evidence.claim: The surrounding cliffs record another kind of movement: the Keystone Thrust forced older gray sedimentary rocks over younger red rocks.
evidence.quote: The movement of this fault forced the older gray sedimentary rock over the younger red rocks

evidence.claim: That contact is exposed for 13 miles along the escarpment.
evidence.quote: The thrust is exposed over a distance of 13 miles (21 km) along the Red Rock escarpment.

evidence.claim: The Aztec Sandstone began as immense desert dunes, later cemented with calcium carbonate and iron oxides into the rock seen here.
evidence.quote: These dunes accumulated over a broad area, up to 0.5 miles (0.80 km) thick, and were lithified, cemented with calcium carbonate and iron oxides. They developed as the colorful Aztec Sandstone.

evidence.claim: For the Scenic Loop, a timed-entry reservation is required each day from October 1 through May 31 for entry between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m.
evidence.quote: Visitors must have a timed entry reservation for each day they plan to enter, October 1 to May 31, 8am -5pm.

evidence.claim: A spring-fed creek and grassy meadows made this a campsite for travelers on the alternate Spanish Trail route through Cottonwood Valley.
evidence.quote: The spring-fed creek and grassy meadows formed an oasis for travelers using the alternate route of the Spanish Trail through Cottonwood Valley.

evidence.claim: Camping began in the mid-1830s; pack and wagon trains continued using the site until the railroad replaced them in 1905.
evidence.quote: In the mid-1830s, a campsite was established along the wash that runs through the ranch.

evidence.claim: pack and wagon trains continued using the site until the railroad replaced them in 1905.
evidence.quote: The use of the site by pack and wagon trains continued until their replacement by the railroad in 1905.

evidence.claim: James B. Wilson and George Anderson established Sandstone Ranch in 1876.
evidence.quote: Sand Stone Ranch, as it was first known, was formed in 1876 by Sergeant James B. Wilson and George Anderson.

evidence.claim: The cattle ranch later became a retreat.
evidence.quote: Over time it transformed from the working ranch to a retreat.

evidence.claim: Later owners included Chester Lauck, Vera Krupp and Howard Hughes.
evidence.quote: Later owners included; Chester Lauck (1948), Vera Krupp (1955) and Howard Hughes.

evidence.claim: The state park preserves the ranch, including its main house, blacksmith's shop, barn, corral and chinchilla shed.
evidence.quote: Historical sites at the park include the main ranch house, cabin and bunkhouse, blacksmith's shop, barn and corral, two-hole outhouse, chinchilla shed, and Wilson family cemetery.

evidence.claim: The preserved property also includes a cabin, bunkhouse and Wilson family cemetery.
evidence.quote: Historical sites at the park include the main ranch house, cabin and bunkhouse, blacksmith's shop, barn and corral, two-hole outhouse, chinchilla shed, and Wilson family cemetery.

evidence.claim: Notice the ranch buildings, including the blacksmith's shop and chinchilla shed.
evidence.quote: Historical sites at the park include the main ranch house, cabin and bunkhouse, blacksmith's shop, barn and corral, two-hole outhouse, chinchilla shed

evidence.claim: Blue Diamond grew as a company town after gypsum processing moved closer to the mine.
evidence.quote: In 1941, Blue Diamond added a processing plant on-site for the gypsum, which had previously been processed in Los Angeles.

evidence.claim: The plant opened in 1941, and the company began building the town the following year.
evidence.quote: The company opened a wallboard manufacturing plant at the site in 1941, and then began building a company town in 1942.

evidence.claim: Gypsum mined at the top of Blue Diamond Hill traveled by tram to the processing area at the bottom.
evidence.quote: Gypsum was mined at the top of Blue Diamond Hill and was transported by tram to the area below, where it was processed.

evidence.claim: The village of Cottonwood briefly became Blue Diamondville before taking the name Blue Diamond later in 1942.
evidence.quote: The village of Cottonwood became known as Blue Diamondville that year, when a post office opened under that name. The name was changed to Blue Diamond later in the year

evidence.claim: Its general store, built in 1942 for a community composed mostly of miners, retains its original exterior appearance.
evidence.quote: The mercantile (general store) was built in 1942 and originally sold household staples and sundries to residents who were mostly miners at the Blue Diamond Mine. The store has maintained its original external look.

evidence.claim: Historical photographs supplied by the Blue Diamond Historical Society hang inside.
evidence.quote: Walls inside the store showcase many of the town's historical photos, courtesy of the Blue Diamond Historical Society

flags: SR 159 scenic segment (approximately 8.8 miles), full numbered route (19.180 miles in cache), material mapped route (19.9 miles), and separate 13-mile Scenic Loop are distinct. Reservation note applies only to the loop.
